story.title: Omani Agriculture Day Marks 4.2 Million Tons of Annual Food Production

detail.extracted_title: Omani Agriculture Day Marks 4.2 Million Tons of Annual Food Production
detail.excerpt: Backed by 3,000 living aflaj channels and the "Reefy" rural women's program, Oman's farm and fisheries output now exceeds RO 1.8 billion in market value
detail.article_html:
For millennia, farming in the Sultanate of Oman has depended on an exact pact between human engineering and scarce mountain water. From Copper Age stone settlements and terraced wadis to more than 3,000 living aflaj irrigation channels that still gravity-feed oases today, Omani growers historically supplied Indian Ocean ports with dried dates, Omani limes, pomegranates, mangoes, and frankincense. As the Sultanate celebrates Omani Agriculture Day across its governorates, new national figures show how that ancestral agrarian foundation has scaled into a modern food-security engine.

In an analytical review of the sector's trajectory since 1970, Dr. Hamed bin Said Al Oufi, former Minister of Agriculture and Fisheries, detailed how the combined gross domestic product of Oman's agricultural and fisheries sectors climbed from RO 17 million in 1970 to more than RO 1 billion in 2025. Over the same period, total domestic food production across crops, livestock, and fisheries expanded from less than 300,000 tons a year to more than 4.2 million tons in 2025, generating a market value exceeding RO 1.8 billion.

Three Hundred Thousand Cultivated Feddans and 3,000 Active Aflaj

That fourteen-fold expansion in physical food output rests on sustained investment in water efficiency, soil research, and high-yield seed varieties. Across the Sultanate, total cultivated farmland has grown by more than 300 percent since 1970 to surpass 300,000 feddans, irrigated by modern pressurized systems, groundwater recharge dams, and over 3,000 active aflaj channels.

Rather than relying solely on seasonal open-field cultivation, Omani farms increasingly deploy climate-controlled greenhouses, hydroponics, and tissue-culture laboratories that propagate disease-resistant date palms alongside high-altitude crops in Al Jabal Al Akhdar and subtropical fruits across the Dhofar coastal plain. Simultaneously, the national livestock herd has grown to more than 3.7 million heads of camels, cattle, sheep, and goats, anchored by industrial-scale food-security projects including Mazoon Dairy in Al Sunaynah, Al Murooj Dairy in Dhofar, and large-scale poultry and egg production complexes.

Empowering Omani Rural Women Through the "Reefy" Program

A defining feature of this year's Omani Agriculture Day celebrations is the recognition of Omani rural women as primary producers and food-manufacturing entrepreneurs. In South Al Batinah Governorate, celebrations in Rustaq under the patronage of Governor Eng. Masoud bin Said Al Hashmi brought together 22 specialized exhibition corners highlighting female rural entrepreneurs, mountain apiaries, date processors, and smart irrigation startups.

Through the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Water Resources' "Reefy" (My Countryside) program, rural women receive targeted micro-financing, food-safety certification, modern packaging design, and direct retail access. Instead of selling raw milk, honey, or dates at farm-gate wholesale prices, women-led rural enterprises now process and brand artisanal cheeses, clarified ghee, distilled rosewater, moringa oils, and value-added date confections—retaining higher margins inside mountain and desert villages.

Climate Resilience and Biosecurity for the Next Decade

Even as domestic self-sufficiency rises across dairy, poultry, dates, and seasonal vegetables, the sector faces persistent environmental pressures, including groundwater salinity in coastal plains, rising temperatures, and transboundary plant pests such as the red palm weevil and dubas bug. Addressing these pressures requires expanding treated-wastewater irrigation, solar-powered desalination for coastal farms, and drone-based crop monitoring—ensuring that Oman's 3,000 aflaj and modern agro-industrial estates continue feeding generations to come.

Sources

  • Oman Daily
detail.instagram_caption:
As the Sultanate marks Omani Agriculture Day across its governorates, national production figures highlight how centuries of terraced mountain farming and ancient aflaj engineering have scaled into a modern food-security pillar.

From under 300,000 tons of annual production in 1970, Oman's combined agricultural, livestock, and fisheries output has surpassed 4.2 million tons in 2025, generating a market value exceeding RO 1.8 billion and contributing over RO 1 billion to national GDP:

- 300,000+ Cultivated Feddans: Farmland across the Sultanate has expanded by over 300 percent, irrigated by modern pressurized networks and more than 3,000 living aflaj channels.
- 3.7 Million Livestock & Dairy Hubs: National herds of camels, cattle, sheep, and goats have topped 3.7 million heads, supported by major food-security enterprises such as Mazoon Dairy in Al Sunaynah and Al Murooj Dairy in Dhofar.
- Rural Women & The "Reefy" Program: Across governorate celebrations—including a 22-booth showcase in Rustaq—the "Reefy" program equips Omani rural women with financing, packaging, and market access to turn raw honey, dairy, rosewater, and dates into branded consumer goods.

Read the full feature on Oman's agricultural evolution at omanspire.om (link in bio).

seo_metadata.featured_image_alt_text: Minimalist Swiss serigraph editorial illustration of terraced Omani mountain farms, date palms, and a marine-teal falaj channel with an Omani farmer and rural woman.
seo_metadata.visual_prompt: Minimalist mid-century Swiss serigraph and lineless faceted geometric editorial illustration celebrating Omani Agriculture Day, ancient aflaj irrigation channels, and rural food security. Monumental, surreal conceptual composition where sweeping origami-faceted mountain agricultural terraces in warm desert sand ochre and burnt terracotta step upward toward towering geometric date palm silhouettes, while a luminous marine-teal falaj water channel cuts diagonally across the terraced landscape under dramatic diagonal chiaroscuro shadow planes against a deep midnight navy and cream off-white sky. In small environmental scale, minimalist faceless geometric silhouettes of an Omani farmer in a crisp off-white dishdasha and embroidered kumma cap and an Omani rural woman in a modest flowing black abaya and shayla headscarf tending geometric terracotta harvest vessels along the stone falaj bank. Strictly lineless flat color planes with zero black comic outlines, zero facial features, zero floating arrows or glowing tablets, and subtle screenprint risograph paper grain texture. Curated high-contrast palette of deep midnight navy shadows, warm desert sand ochre, burnt terracotta coral, clean cream off-white, and a focused accent of marine teal. High-end New Yorker, Economist, and Monocle magazine cover art aesthetic. Strictly no realism, no text, no words, no letters, no typography, no labels, no signs, no numbers baked into the artwork, strictly no frame, no border, no white margin, no matting, seamless full bleed composition extending to all four edges.
